newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH GOVT AND SAMSUNG NEGOTIATE FOKKER RELAUNCH.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH GOVT AND SAMSUNG NEGOTIATE FOKKER RELAUNCH.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Aerospace and delegates of Dutch Economics Minister Hans Wijers on Wednesday kicked off negotiations on the relaunch of bankrupt planemaker Fokker.
Former Unilever chairman Floris Maljers was leading the negotiations on behalf of the minister, an Economics Ministry spokesman said.
"The negotiations started today. Maljers has been asked because of his expert business knowledge," he said.
Samsung last week presented the government with a business plan which forms the basis of the negotiations.
The location of the talks was kept top secret in an anxious bid to ward off media attention.

Dozens of Dutch journalists follow the attempts to resuscitate the aviation pioneer which collapsed on March 15, two months after its German parent Daimler Benz Aerospace no longer wanted to carry Fokker's huge losses.
Its bankruptcy triggered the biggest mass redundancy in the Dutch industrial history as many thousands lost their jobs.
Maljers also mediated on behalf of the government earlier this year when he tried to work out a deal with Daimler, but he then failed to get negotations off the ground.
The talks with Samsung are expected to be concluded in several weeks as Fokker's receivers have already told the remaining staff that they have a deadline of end-October.
That is the moment that suppliers of components such as aircraft bodies, wings and engines need to know whether they should dismantle their production lines for Fokker parts.
Since its demise, Fokker has continued production of aircraft with some 650 assembly workers. It has even accepted new orders to help preserve the value of assets.
The Economics Ministry said it was not bound by a deadline, but confirmed that time for a relaunch was limited.

Terms for the negotiations have not been made public, but sources close to the talks said Samsung had asked the Dutch government for 450 million guilders in aircraft development subsidies, around one third of the 1.2 billion guilders needed to develop a new 130-seater jet, later to be produced in Korea.
Samsung wants the Dutch state to allow a new leasing company to carry forward 300 million guilders of tax-deductable losses.
Additionally, the Dutch state should take a 15 percent equity stake in the new Fokker, costing 15 million guilders.
A subordinated loan of 100 million guilders and a 40 million launch subsidy would complete the government's contribution.
Samsung in its turn would pay 250-300 million for Fokker's assets, worth over a billion guilders at the time of the bankruptcy, and take a 75 percent stake in the new company.
It would further cough up 400 million guilders for the aircraft leasing company and invest 755 million in the new aircraft development programme.
If Samsung and the Dutch government strike a deal, jobs at the F70 and F100 assembly lines will be safe until 2006-2010, the remaining life of these planes, sources said.
